analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers to give up their day in court and their right to join class actions.
analysis.headline: 17 senators backed the bill to end forced arbitration at work, but it has received no action since being referred to the Senate labor committee in July 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unenforceable for employers to require workers, as a condition of a job, to arbitrate work disputes or to give up the right to join class or collective lawsuits. Arbitration could still happen after a dispute, but only if the worker freely agrees in writing, after a 45-day waiting period and plain-language notice, without any threat of retaliation. It would also change the National Labor Relations Act so employers cannot force workers to waive their right to act together, and it covers independent contractors no matter how the employer labels them.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers regain the right to take disputes over pay, firing, discrimination, and other workplace matters to court, and to join class or collective actions, which is often the only affordable way to pursue a small-dollar claim. Lower-paid and nonunion workers are the most affected because they are the most likely to be covered by mandatory arbitration clauses. Independent contractors, including gig workers, are covered no matter how the employer classifies them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers bound by mandatory arbitration clauses

how_it_helps.text: Voids predispute arbitration agreements that require arbitration of work disputes.
Voids predispute waivers of joint, class, or collective actions, restoring workers' ability to sue together.

Permits postdispute arbitration only for truly voluntary agreements: no coercion or threat of adverse action, plain-language written notice of the right to refuse without retaliation, a 45-day waiting period, and affirmative written consent.

Amends the National Labor Relations Act so it is an unfair labor practice to require, coerce, or retaliate over a worker's promise not to pursue a joint, class, or collective claim, and makes such agreements void.
Gives workers a civil action, with attorney's fees, against employers who retaliate for refusing to arbitrate, and tolls the statute of limitations during the 45-day waiting period.
Covers independent contractors regardless of the label the company uses, and applies even to domestic service work in households.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially large ones, lose the arbitration clauses that currently steer work disputes into a private forum without class actions, and arbitration providers lose the employment caseload. Some employers and small businesses would face more litigation in court, which is typically slower and more expensive per dispute than arbitration.

drawbacks.text: By allowing predispute arbitration only when chosen after a dispute arises, the bill pushes workplace disputes into court, which is generally slower and costlier than arbitration, and the legal defense and litigation costs fall on employers — including small businesses — and partly on consumers through prices.

The bill does not require employers to offer any alternative dispute process, so some workers who previously had a fast, low-cost arbitration forum for small claims would instead need to litigate in court or forgo their claim.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers most affected, the ability to sue together is usually decisive: small wage-theft or discrimination claims are rarely worth pursuing alone, which is why mass arbitration bans effectively erase many rights. The main real cost is slower, pricier dispute resolution for employers and for workers with claims they would rather arbitrate quickly. On balance the bill trades a cheaper private process for a stronger, public one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate's labor committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the Restoring Justice for Workers Act on July 30, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — has been taken since the referral.

The bill's findings state that millions of workers must accept arbitration and class-action waivers as a condition of work, often without realizing it, and that individual arbitration deters workers from seeking any remedy at all because of well-founded fear of retaliation.
17 senators cosponsored the bill: 15 of the Senate's 45 Democrats and both of its independents; no Republican has cosponsored.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, large employers and arbitration providers, because the mandatory arbitration clauses and class-action waivers they rely on remain fully enforceable while the bill sits unacted on in committee. If the bill dies this session, those interests will be the ones better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers and arbitration providers, so far

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on July 30, 2026.

against.name: Bill Cassidy
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee hearing, markup, or vote since it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors are Democrats or independents and no Republican has signed on; the bill sits in a committee controlled by the Senate's 55-member Republican majority, which has taken no action on it.

industries.note: Most large employers use mandatory arbitration clauses that block court suits and class actions over pay, firing, and discrimination; the bill voids those clauses for future disputes, so workplace claims would move to open court.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers (AAA, JAMS, and private arbitrators)
industries.note: Employment disputes are a large share of arbitration caseload; with predispute work-dispute arbitration voided, that business moves back into the court system.
The bill covers workers engaged as independent contractors regardless of the label the company uses, so platforms cannot rely on contractor status to escape the ban.
The bill adds NLRA protection for concerted claims and keeps the long-standing union-carveout for collective bargaining agreements intact, reinforcing the union arbitration framework.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and the bill having drawn no Republican cosponsor in its first five months, it is unlikely to get a committee markup or a floor vote before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027; the realistic path is reintroduction in a future Congress.
